intro.title: Fairness in Hiring
intro.lede: How should an algorithm decide who gets a job offer?
intro.p1: A company wants to hire only applicants who would perform well in the role. Every hiring decision is therefore also a decision about value and cost.
intro.p2: A model calculates a suitability score for each application. A decision threshold sets the score from which a job offer is made.
intro.p3: The dataset contains 400 fictional applications from two groups: Pinkville and Greenfield. Each group has 100 suitable and 100 unsuitable applicants. Yet the scores are distributed differently in the two groups.
intro.p4: You take the role of a fairness advisor: first look at the two applicant groups, then decide where the decision thresholds should be.
intro.note: All people and places are fictional. The data and the €300/€700 values are a simplified model.
intro.start: Start with the two applicant groups
intro.valueText: A suitable hire creates €300 in value; an unsuitable hire costs €700. The numbers are a simplified model.
intro.scoreText: Score ≥ threshold: job offer. Score < threshold: no job offer.
intro.dataText: 400 applications from two groups. Each group has 100 suitable and 100 unsuitable applicants.

twoPopulations.title: Two Applicant Groups
twoPopulations.subtitle: What is in the data?
twoPopulations.intro1: The dataset contains 400 applications: 200 from people in Pinkville and 200 from Greenfield.
twoPopulations.intro2: Each group has 100 suitable and 100 unsuitable applicants. The starting point is therefore the same.
twoPopulations.intro3: The scores, however, differ: applications from Pinkville receive higher suitability scores on average than applications from Greenfield.
twoPopulations.intro4: This raises the fairness question: what does it mean when a model evaluates two groups differently even though suitability is equally distributed?
twoPopulations.scoreHint: The score ranges from 0 to 100. The higher the score, the more likely the person is suitable for the job.
twoPopulations.taskA: Describe the differences between the two distributions. How can you tell them apart?
twoPopulations.taskB: Why might a single decision threshold be unfair? What should a fair decision take into account?

fairThresholds.title: Fair Decision Thresholds!?
fairThresholds.lede: You are a fairness advisor. Set the rules for hiring.
fairThresholds.intro: The two charts show the suitability scores of the two groups separately. Use the sliders to set the score from which a job offer is made. You can choose different thresholds for the two groups — or a single shared threshold.
fairThresholds.ruleText: If an application's score is at or above the threshold, the person gets a job offer. If it is below, they do not.
fairThresholds.measuresIntro: The confusion matrix counts how many decisions are correct and incorrect. Four metrics are calculated from it:
fairThresholds.confusionHint: In the confusion matrix, the rows are actual suitability and the columns are the model's prediction.
fairThresholds.strategyQuestion: How should Greenfield's threshold be set?
fairThresholds.strategyHint: The three “Same …” strategies set Greenfield's threshold automatically. With “Independent”, you can set it yourself.
fairThresholds.approximateHint: Scores are discrete. “Same offer rates” and “same hit rates” can therefore often only be approximated.
fairThresholds.task1: Try the four strategies. Describe what changes for the two groups.
fairThresholds.task2: Which thresholds do you choose? Write down both values and explain your choice.
fairThresholds.task3a: Which metrics mattered most in your choice? Why?
fairThresholds.task3b: Is your choice fair? If yes, why? If not, what would be a fair choice?
fairThresholds.task3c: What is the most important argument for your choice?

about.title: About This Learning Activity
about.articleDescription: The underlying learning activity is based on the following peer-reviewed article on credit scoring, published in Teaching Statistics:
about.articleCitation: Schönbrodt, S., Schneider, S., Podworny, S., & Camminady, T. (2026). A learning activity on fairness in data-driven algorithmic decision-making systems. Teaching Statistics, 48, 33–44.
about.goalText: This short version focuses on two questions: how do the suitability scores of the two applicant groups differ, and which decision thresholds are defensible from a fairness perspective?
about.shortVersionNote: This website is the short version of the full learning activity. It contains the two interactive chapters on applicant groups and fair decision thresholds.

about.privacyText:
This site does not use cookies or tracking. No data is transmitted to a server.

Only the selected language (fairness.lang) and your notes (fairness.notes.*) are stored locally in your browser. This data does not leave your device. You can remove your notes at any time with “Clear notes”; the language choice remains until you clear your browser data.

The site does not load external fonts or analytics tools.
about.adaptationNote: This short version adapts the idea to hiring. The study itself examines fairness in credit scoring.

measures.defAccuracy: Accuracy: Share of correct decisions out of all applications.
measures.defPositiveRate: Offer rate: Share of applications that receive a job offer (prediction: offer) out of all applications.
measures.defTruePositiveRate: Hit rate: Share of suitable applicants who actually receive a job offer.
measures.defValue: Value: €300 for every successful hire minus €700 for every unsuitable hire.
